docs.title: Based Datatypes Docs
docs.text:
Welcome! 👋

This documentation covers the based-datatypes project: a small, dependency-light library of shared Python types, typing helpers and data utilities.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
The package is not published on PyPI yet; install it from the Git remote:

uv add "based-datatypes @ git+https://github.com/cloudlane-one/based-datatypes.git"

Requires Python 3.13 or newer.

docs.title: Usage guides
docs.text:
Each module has a task-oriented guide with runnable examples. Every guide links the matching section of the Python API reference instead of repeating signatures and docstrings.

  • Enums String enums that render as their value in docs and logs.

  • Types and protocols Nominal strings, state markers, structural protocols and shared aliases.

  • Context variables Scoped context values with guaranteed restoration.

  • Runtime reflection Calling module, call arguments, return types and subclass trees.

  • Type reflection Resolve, compare and map type hints — including generic classes that remember their arguments.

  • Hashing Stable hashes of dataclasses, containers, functions and dataframes.

  • Data utilities Dataclass copying, container conversion and mapping flattening.

  • Files and directories One interface for single files and directory trees, with MIME types and typed streams.

  • Serialization Move objects through JSON, YAML, parquet, arrays, images and more — selected by format, scope and losslessness.

  • Descriptors Typed, cacheable properties and dual-dispatch methods.

  • Object references Persistent, URL-serialisable pointers to Python objects.

  • Distributions Which distribution or Git repository a module belongs to.

docs.title: Choosing third-party deps
docs.text:
There are many aspects to consider when choosing which third-party packages to rely on. Bad things can happen, if choices are not made wisely, as perfectly illustrated by this XKCD comic:

Arguably the most important aspect is whether packages currently have known vulnerabilities. Accordingly, a whole fleet of tools and platforms exists for scanning your deps to that end, some freely usable. For looking up singular packages online, any one of these is good for use:

  • LFX-Insights: Curated info on popular code projects
  • deps.dev: Exhaustive info on Python and other packages
  • Snyk Advisor: Exhaustive info on Python and other packages

vulnerability = bug or backdoor in the source code, which can be used by an attacker to disturb the software, get unallowed access or steal data

For Python packages specifically, an open-source tool exists for scanning all your dependencies for vulnerabilities at once: pip-audit, which is in fact used within this repo.

Beyond that, package health in terms of maintenance and code quality is another important signal, that ideally serves to prevent vulnerabilities alltogether.

docs.title: Installing dependencies
docs.text:
All dependency installation should be done using uv. See the official docs for details. Tl;dr: uv add PACKAGE_NAME to add it to the core library dependencies, uv add --group GROUP_NAME PACKAGE_NAME to add it to a specific group.

See /pyproject.toml for a list of all dependency groups with descriptions in the comments.

docs.title: How to check quality
docs.text: Certain checks are run by VSCode automatically as you edit code, while others have to be run manually using VSCode UI, tasks or commands in the terminal.

docs.title: Automatic checks
docs.text:
• Linting via ruff
  • Type-checking via pyright

Discovered issues by these tools will show up as yellow or red squiggly lines underlining your code.

docs.title: Manual checks
docs.text:
Pytest test cases can be run via the VSCode tests UI (beaker symbol in left sidebar) or uv run pytest tests in the terminal.

VSCode tasks can be run via the UI by clicking ctrl + shift + P to open the command palette and then typing Run task, or in the terminal via vtr TASK_NAME. Please run all tasks with the prefixes assert-, build- and info-. Make sure none of them fail and that their printed information does not hint at any major issues.

docs.title: Scoped context variables
docs.text: based_datatypes.context provides set_ctx_var, a context manager that sets a contextvars.ContextVar for a block and restores the previous value afterwards — including when the block raises.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text: Use it instead of manual token = var.set(...) / var.reset(token) pairs whenever the value is scoped to a with block: request identifiers, per-operation log context, feature flags during a test.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text: inside: req-42 req-42 outside: none

docs.title: Nesting and restoration
docs.text:
Blocks unwind in order, so the value of the enclosing scope returns when an inner block exits.

inner: 2 middle: 1 outer: 0

An exception does not leave a stale value behind:

False

docs.title: API
docs.text: Outside the set_ctx_var helper demonstrated above, the module has no public names; see the API reference for its signature.

docs.title: Contexts stay isolated
docs.text:
ContextVar values are per-context, and the helper only touches the context it runs in. A copy taken before the block keeps the old value, which is what asyncio tasks rely on.

current: 7 copied: 0

Generators keep their context

The helper is a generator-based context manager. Do not yield out of the with block inside a generator that outlives it; the value would remain set for the caller.

docs.title: Types of Contributions
docs.text:
The nature of a contribution roughly aligns with the folders/files, in which it happens, and can be divided into 5 types:

  1. Refactoring contributions may add/modify any files in the repository, but are not allowed to change the public interface of modules in /src or applications in /app, nor make content changes to anything in /docs. This may be ensured by not changing any code in /tests during refactoring, though this is not a requirement.
  2. Documentation contributions only add/modify files in /docs.
  3. Library contributions add/modify modules in /src and may include Documentation contributions related to the changes in /src. Additionally, they must add cases in /tests/src to cover at least 90 % of the contributed code.
  4. Application contributions add/modify notebook scripts (in the form of Jupytext) in /app. These may be rather abstract interfaces for general use of library code, or manifest very specific use cases including elaborate explanations within the notebooks. They may include Library contributions required by respective applications. Additionally, they must add cases in /tests/app to cover at least 90 % of the contributed code.
  5. Major Upgrade contributions include larger, breaking changes to the repository, and as such are not restricted in what they add/modify. However, these contributions will trigger a major version change and thus need to be coordinated carefully with the maintainers.

docs.title: Pull Requests
docs.text:
Any contribution should be made via forking the repo / branching off main and later merging all changes back using a Pull Request (PR) (or Merge Request (MR) on GitLab). Every PR should have a single contribution type (see above), which has to be mentioned at the beginning of the PR title like so:

<Contribution type>: <Rest of your title>

If multiple types apply to your contribution, pick the one with the highest number in the list above.

For the rest of the PR description, please use the PR template.

docs.title: Developing locally
docs.text: Please refer to the local setup guide to get started with working on your local copy of the repo.

docs.title: Commits and Issues
docs.text: Larger contributions / PRs should be split into multiple commits with their own types according to the Gitmoji Spec. If a commit addresses an existing Issue on GitHub / GitLab / etc., please reference that issue via #<ISSUE_ID> somewhere in the commit message. If it resolves the issue (meaning it should be closed), add a footer line to the commit message with Closes:, Fixes:, or Resolves: followed by the issue reference. Make sure you plan ahead how to split up your contribution into commits and in which order.

docs.title: Writing Good Code
docs.text: Please adhere to coding conventions and use tooling as described in this reference. In case you plan on adding any new external (pip) dependencies, please refer to this guide in doing so. Finally, once you are ready to push your code and make a pull request, please make sure you check its quality locally first according to this guide.

docs.title: The Complete Workflow
docs.text:
The entire workflow for making a contribution goes roughly as follows:

  1. Create a fork or banch to work in.
  2. Clone your fork / branch and open it in VSCode.
  3. Install all recommended extensions.
  4. Install/update dependencies via the VSCode task update-dependencies.
  5. Make one or more commits adhering to Gitmoji Spec.
  6. Run local checks and make sure all pass.
  7. Push your commits and make a PR with a title conforming to above spec and description according to the PR template.
  8. Have a kind interaction with the maintainers in the PR comments, get approval, and merge 😊.

docs.title: Dataclass and container utilities
docs.text: based_datatypes.data turns dataclasses into plain mappings, flattens nested mappings, and re-constructs dataclasses while overriding a few fields. It is the plumbing behind config merging, change detection and "copy this record with one value changed" flows.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• copy_and_override: build a modified copy of an immutable or frozen dataclass.
  • container_to_dict: feed a dataclass or pydantic model to code that expects a dict.
  • flatten_dict: turn nested configuration into flat tuple keys for diffing or logging.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text: Server(host='api.example.com', port=8080, tags=['prod']) Server(host='api.example.com', port=9090, tags=['prod']) True

docs.title: Re-constructing a dataclass
docs.text:
copy_and_override(init, obj, *args, **kwargs) reads every field the source defines, applies the positional and keyword overrides, and calls the constructor. Sources may be a single instance or a tuple of instances; later sources win.

Point(x=9, y=2) Point(x=5, y=6)

Fields that are not part of the constructor (init=False, e.g. derived values) are copied after construction:

Doubled(value=3, double=6)

docs.title: Generic constructors and MaskedInit
docs.text:
When the constructor carries type parameters, MaskedInit pairs the constructor's type with the runtime class, so the call site stays typed:

Box(item=2)

Known limitations

Keyword-only dataclasses and InitVar fields are not supported: the source values are passed positionally. Required fields missing from every source raise, rather than being silently defaulted.

docs.title: Converting containers to dicts
docs.text:
container_to_dict recognises dataclass instances, pydantic models, mappings, sequences and sets. Every other object yields None.

{Attr(name='name'): 'ada', Attr(name='roles'): {0: 'admin'}} {0: 10, 1: 20} None

Dataclass keys become Attr instances, so they cannot collide with the string keys of a mapping that was converted inside the same structure. Recursion is on by default; pass recursive=False to keep nested objects untouched.

{Attr(name='inner'): {Attr(name='value'): 1}}

Self-referencing containers terminate: the recursive branch maps back to the result object already built for that container.

True

docs.title: Flattening nested mappings
docs.text:
flatten_dict walks mappings only; sequences are values, not paths. The result maps a tuple of keys to the leaf value.

{('server', 'host'): 'localhost', ('server', 'ports'): [80, 443], ('debug',): True}

Cycle handling

A self-reference resolves to the partially-built result for that mapping, so it contributes no extra leaf. The output therefore omits the recursive key entirely rather than emitting an empty path.

Signatures and docstrings for copy_and_override, container_to_dict, flatten_dict and MaskedInit are in the API reference.

docs.title: Properties and dual-dispatch methods
docs.text:
based_datatypes.descriptors provides two descriptors:

  • prop: a typed property that can be an instance property, a class property, or both, and that can cache its value.
  • dualmethod: a method that works when called on an instance and on the class.

Both exist because the builtin property / classmethod combinations are hard to type and easy to get subtly wrong.

docs.title: When to use prop
docs.text:
• A computed value that should behave like an attribute (@prop).
  • A constant derived from the class, reachable as Model.timeout (mode="class").
  • A value computed per instance exactly once (cached=True).
  • An attribute that needs a setter and/or deleter without boilerplate.

docs.title: Instance properties
docs.text:
@prop is the default, instance-mode form. Reading it on the class returns the descriptor itself, just like property.

12.566 prop area

Setters and deleters use the familiar decorator pattern. Declaring writable=True or deletable=True without the corresponding function fails at class creation, so a half-implemented property cannot reach production.

10

docs.title: Class and dual properties
docs.text:
mode="class" evaluates against the class (works from instances too). mode="dual" passes whichever object was used to access it, so one implementation can serve both.

https://api.example.com https://api.example.com class instance

docs.title: Caching
docs.text:
cached=True computes the value once and reuses it. Assigning or deleting through the property drops the cache; with a setter the value is then recomputed from the new state.

1 1 1 7 2

The instance cache holds strong references

Cached instance values are stored per property, keyed by instance identity, and the entry keeps the instance alive. Do not use cached=True for a property on a class with a very large number of short-lived instances; use an explicit cache with a policy instead.

Class caches are per class

A subclass parameterised differently gets its own cached class value.

docs.title: Dual-dispatch methods
docs.text:
dualmethod wraps a function whose first parameter is annotated Self | type[Self]. The descriptor passes the instance when called through an instance and the class when called through the class.

class Factory instance primary

Annotate the first parameter

The implementation receives either a class or an instance, so its first parameter must be annotated ClassName | type[ClassName] for the type checker to accept the descriptor. A plain self: ClassName annotation is rejected — the call would not be type-safe through the class.

docs.title: Cached methods
docs.text:
cached_method is the method-level counterpart of cached=True: it memoises the result per instance, keyed by the arguments (and by the decorated function, so an override and the base implementation it calls through super() do not share a result). The cache lives in the instance's __dict__, so the class must allow attribute assignment.

2 3 2 3 2

docs.title: Marker classes
docs.text:
Read, Write, Delete and RWD are capability markers used in prop's typing. They form a small hierarchy (Write and Delete derive from Read, RWD from both) and are exported for annotations in downstream code.

Signatures and docstrings for everything in this guide are in the API reference.

docs.title: Reflecting installed distributions
docs.text:
based_datatypes.dist answers questions about the Python environment: which distributions are installed, which distribution a module belongs to, which Git repository a module lives in, and what a distribution's project metadata points at.

It is the low-level half of based_datatypes.ref; use it directly when you need environment facts without building an object reference.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• Map a module (or file) back to the distribution that owns it.
  • Resolve a module to its Git work tree.
  • Read Project-URL metadata (documentation, repository, changelog).
  • Download and parse a Sphinx objects.inv inventory.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text: pandas 3.1.0

docs.title: API
docs.text: The module is a set of functions over modules and distributions: get_distributions, get_module_file, get_module_distribution, get_file_repo, get_module_repo, get_project_urls and get_py_inventory. Each is demonstrated in the sections below, and their signatures are in the API reference.

docs.title: Installed distributions
docs.text:
get_distributions indexes every installed distribution by its metadata name. Import metadata can be unreadable for a broken installation; those entries are skipped rather than raising.

True True True

docs.title: Which distribution owns a module
docs.text:
get_module_distribution compares the module's file path with every distribution's location. The most specific match wins: an editable install points at the repository root, which also contains the virtual environment, so a naive first match would claim every module in site-packages.

True True None

docs.title: Repository lookup
docs.text:
get_file_repo searches parent directories for a Git work tree, so a module deep inside a package still resolves. get_module_repo is the module-level convenience.

True True

A file outside any repository returns None; no exception is raised.

docs.title: Project URLs
docs.text:
get_project_urls reads the Project-URL metadata entries and matches the key exactly. Keys are conventionally Documentation, Repository, Changelog, API Reference.

repository: [] missing key: []

docs.title: Object inventories
docs.text:
get_py_inventory downloads <docs_url>/objects.inv, parses it with Sphinx, and merges the py: namespaces into one mapping. It is cached per URL, because inventories are large and rarely change during a process lifetime.

see the commented example

HTTP errors propagate

get_py_inventory calls raise_for_status(), so a 404 or a network failure raises instead of returning an empty mapping. Wrap the call when the documentation URL comes from untrusted input.

Version checks and outdated dependencies live in ref

get_versions_on_pypi, get_outdated_deps and version_diff are in based_datatypes.ref; they combine distribution metadata with PyPI requests and are documented in Object references.

docs.title: Enums that read well in docs and logs
docs.text: based_datatypes.enums provides one class, StrEnum, a drop-in replacement for enum.StrEnum. Its only difference is presentation: a member renders as its value everywhere, including in repr, so generated API docs, logs and tracebacks show 'red' instead of <Color.red: 'red'>.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text: Use it for every string enum in a project that documents its enums (mkdocstrings, Sphinx) or logs enum values, and especially where members are parsed from configuration files.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text: 'red' red red!

docs.title: API
docs.text: StrEnum and parse are the module's whole public surface; see the API reference for their signatures and docstrings. parse is a typed counterpart of calling the enum itself.

docs.title: Members behave like strings
docs.text:
A member is a str subclass, so it compares equal to its value, serialises as that value, and can be used as a mapping key.

True

docs.title: Parsing configuration values
docs.text:
parse is the typed counterpart of calling the enum: it keeps the subclass type, so code that receives a Color keeps receiving a Color.

ValueError 'blue' is not a valid Color

No fuzzy parsing

parse matches values exactly. Case folding, aliases and prefix matching are policy decisions and belong in the calling code, not in the enum base class.

docs.title: Files and directories
docs.text: based_datatypes.files gives files and directories one small interface, so storage code does not care whether a file lives on the local disk or behind object storage later. A file knows its MIME type and whether it carries text or bytes, and it hands out an open stream on request; a directory behaves like a mapping of names to files and sub-directories.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• Pass a file around (to a serializer, a job, a test fixture) without passing paths and reopening them everywhere.
  • Derive a MIME type and file extension for content you are about to write.
  • Walk, count, or remove a directory tree with the mapping protocol instead of os calls.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
text/plain TextIO text .txt hello

from_path reads the suffix and the file's tags, so a JSON file becomes application/json with a text stream and a .json extension, while a PNG becomes image/png with a binary stream.

docs.title: Reading and writing
docs.text:
open(mode) takes "r", "w" or "rw" and closes the stream when the block ends. Text streams are always UTF-8 and never translate line endings, so the bytes on disk are the same on every platform.

out.json b'{"a": 1}'

get_io(mode) returns the stream without a context manager when you need to hand ownership to another library; you are then responsible for closing it.

docs.title: MIME type and extension
docs.text:
mimetypes cannot name every format a data library cares about, so the module keeps a small supplementary table (.parquet, .npy, .npz, .pkl, .yaml, .xlsx, .sql, ...). The table is consulted first, and the extension is derived from the MIME type when a file is constructed from scratch:

application/vnd.apache.parquet ['.yaml', '.yml'] .csv

A file created by from_path keeps the suffix it actually has; a file you construct yourself gets the canonical extension for its MIME type unless you pass _suffix.

docs.title: Directories
docs.text:
LocalDir is a mapping: keys(), len(), in, [], del and iteration over its entries. Indexing a sub-directory returns another LocalDir, indexing a file returns a LocalFile.

['notes.txt', 'out.json', 'sub'] 3 LocalDir LocalFile[typing.Literal['text/plain'], , typing.Any] text/plain ['notes.txt', 'sub', 'out.json']

directory.file(name) and directory.subdir(name) are typed accessors that assert the kind of entry. Deleting a sub-directory removes the whole tree:

['notes.txt', 'out.json']

Creating a LocalDir for a path that does not exist yet is allowed: the directory is created when you first read or write through it.

docs.title: In-memory files
docs.text:
MemoryFile implements the same interface without touching the disk. It is handy for tests and for staging content before it is written somewhere. Writes are stored back into content when the stream is closed, and "w" / "rw" start from empty content just like a local file:

{"a": 1} .json text

Content must match the declared io_type: a text file takes str, a binary file takes bytes. A read-only stream ("r") rejects writes instead of silently discarding them.

docs.title: Text or binary
docs.text:
Every file carries an io_type (TextIO or BinaryIO) and a detected_format of "text" or "binary". from_path decides from the file's tags, and falls back to the MIME type for a path that does not exist yet. Serializers use this to reject a text target for a binary format before any bytes are written.

The abstract bases File and Dir, the concrete LocalFile, MemoryFile and LocalDir, the MIME tables and ensure_dir_exists are documented in the API reference.

docs.title: Stable hashes of Python objects
docs.text: based_datatypes.hashing computes integers and short hex strings from Python values. The hash depends on the value, not on id(), so it survives pickling, process restarts and re-serialisation of the same data.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
Use it to compare or key data that is not hashable (lists, dicts, dataclasses, dataframes), to cache derived results, or to derive short, readable identifiers for test cases and config snapshots.

Do not use it as a cryptographic digest or as a replacement for hash() in hot paths: it is deterministic, not secret, and slower than hash.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text: True effa9b381c effa9b

docs.title: API
docs.text: gen_int_hash(obj) returns the stable non-negative integer, and gen_str_hash(obj, length=10) its hex rendering. Their signatures are in the API reference.

docs.title: What is supported
docs.text:
Input Behaviour None 0. Modules Hash of the module name. Classes and named aliases Hash of (module, name). Named functions Hash of the function's PyObjectRef URL (module + qualname). Generic aliases and unions Hash of the origin and the arguments. int, float, bool, str, bytes, dates and times Hash of the type and value. tuple, list Ordered composition; a tuple and a list with equal items hash alike. dict Key/value pairs, independent of insertion order. set Members, independent of iteration order. pandas DataFrame, Series, Index pandas.util.hash_pandas_object. polars DataFrame, Series Row and series hashes, when polars is installed. Any other hashable object Its own __hash__ (see the caveat below). Unhashable dataclass Hash of its field mapping. Unhashable object with __getstate__ Hash of the state mappings. Unhashable object with __getnewargs__(_ex) Hash of the constructor arguments.

Anything else raises ValueError.

unsupported

docs.title: Structured data
docs.text:
True

Cycles terminate: a container that references itself contributes 0 at the repeated reference instead of recursing forever.

True

docs.title: Dataframes
docs.text:
pandas objects hash through pandas.util.hash_pandas_object; polars DataFrame and Series values hash through hash_rows() and hash() respectively. The polars branch is skipped when polars cannot be imported.

True True

Identity hashes are not portable

Python's built-in hash() for str is randomised per process, and for most objects it is derived from id(). Because the fallback branch uses __hash__, hashing an object that is neither one of the supported types nor structurally hashable is only stable within a process. Supported types, dataclasses, pandas objects and picklable objects are stable across processes.

Hashable wins over pickling hooks

The fallback order is deliberate: any hashable object uses its __hash__ before the dataclass and __getstate__ branches. Those branches apply to unhashable objects. A class that defines __getstate__ and is also hashable will use __hash__.

docs.title: Short identifiers
docs.text:
gen_str_hash returns the low-order hex digits of the integer hash, left-padded with zeros to the requested length. Truncation makes collisions more likely, so keep the default width unless the identifier is display-only.

'0000000000' '' 52ad06c22d569933

docs.title: Persistent references to Python objects
docs.text:
based_datatypes.ref turns a live Python object into a small, serialisable record that says what the object is and where it came from: module, qualified name, repository (or package index), version range, and the Python version it was resolved under.

The record can be rendered as a URL, parsed back, and used later to import and resolve the same object again — in another process, on another machine, or in a generated document.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text: Use it to build registries, documentation links, experiment provenance, or plugin manifests that must survive a restart. Do not use it as a general serialisation format for object state; it stores a pointer, not the object.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text: PyObjectRef(object_type=, qualname='int', module_name='builtins', repo_url=None, version=None, py_version='~3.14.10', _object=, _module=, _dist=None) py:?python=~3.14.10#builtins:int builtins

docs.title: API
docs.text: PyObjectRef.reference(obj, version=None, version_strategy="major") builds a record from a live object and PyObjectRef.from_url(text, obj_type) parses one back. The record exposes url, module, dist, object and docs_url; stref(obj) is the short module.qualname form. Version arithmetic (version_diff, version_to_range, semver_range_to_spec), get_all_module_dependencies, get_versions_on_pypi and get_outdated_deps live in the same module. Signatures and docstrings are in the API reference.

docs.title: What a reference records
docs.text:
reference inspects the object's module and distribution:

  • Built-in objects get no repository and no version.
  • Objects installed from a distribution get the distribution's version (as a semver range by default) and the PyPI simple index as their repository.
  • Objects belonging to a Git checkout (editable installs, or code that is not packaged) get the checkout's remote URL and either the installed version or the tag/branch name.

pandas DataFrame https://pypi.org/simple/pandas ^3.1.0

Versions that are not semver

If the distribution (or tag) is not a valid semantic version, the reference carries no version unless version_strategy="exact" is used, in which case it pins ==<version>.

docs.title: Rendering and parsing
docs.text:
The URL uses a py: scheme. py+<scheme> records where the code lives, and the query carries the version constraints. The fragment is module:qualname.

py+https://github.com/example/project?version=%5E1.4&python=~3.12#my_package.parsing:Parser.parse https://github.com/example/project ^1.4 ~3.12 my_package.parsing Parser.parse

The fragment is not URL-decoded for display

Nested qualnames (Outer.method) and dots survive the round trip because the fragment is split on the first colon only. Use from_url rather than parsing the string by hand.

docs.title: Resolving later
docs.text:
module imports the module, dist verifies that the installed distribution satisfies the recorded version constraint, and object walks the qualified name and checks the resulting type.

builtins

A wrong object_type is reported, not silently accepted:

TypeError Object builtins.int must have type <class 'str'>

Built-ins skip the distribution check

A reference without a repository (a built-in) has no distribution to verify, so module/object work without an installed package of the same name.

docs.title: Documentation links
docs.text: docs_url looks up the distribution's Project-URL entries. If a Documentation URL is present, its Sphinx objects.inv is searched for the object and the exact anchor is returned when found (otherwise the documentation root). Only when no Documentation URL is declared does it probe an API Reference URL for a matching page. Both discovery steps perform HTTP requests, so cache the result or catch failures at the call site.

docs.title: Short names
docs.text: builtins.int based_datatypes.ref.PyObjectRef

docs.title: Version arithmetic
docs.text:
The helpers are plain functions and can be used independently of references.

1.3.4 None ~1.2.3 <2,>=1.2.3 True

semver_range_to_spec accepts ^ (caret), ~ (tilde), the comparison operators >=, <=, >, <, ==/= and a bare version.

docs.title: Dependencies of a module
docs.text:
get_all_module_dependencies walks the members of a module, classifying each module they come from as external (part of an installed distribution) or internal, and recurses into the internal ones. Cycles are handled, and the module itself is never reported as its own dependency.

external: ['based-datatypes', 'beartype'] False

docs.title: Reflecting the running interpreter
docs.text: based_datatypes.runtime answers four questions about live Python objects: which module called me, which arguments did the caller pass, what does this function return, and which classes derive from this one.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text: These helpers are glue for decorators, dependency-injection containers, plugin registries and diagnostics. They inspect the running process; none of them imports anything.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text: plugins: ['AudioPlugin', 'VideoPlugin']

docs.title: API
docs.text: The four functions are exercised in the sections below. get_calling_module(offset=0) walks up the stack by offset frames, get_full_args_dict(func, args, kwargs=None) fills in defaults, get_return_type(func) reads the annotation unevaluated, and get_subclasses(cls, max_level=None) walks descendants. Signatures and docstrings are in the API reference.

docs.title: Which module called me
docs.text:
False

offset counts frames above the direct caller, which is useful inside a wrapper:

None

docs.title: Reconstructing the caller's arguments
docs.text:
get_full_args_dict maps the parameter names of func to the values supplied in args and kwargs, filling in defaults for parameters that were not passed. It is what a decorator needs to log or forward a call faithfully.

{'retries': 3, 'timeout': 1.5, 'target': 'queue'}

Only declared parameters

Variable positional (*args) and variable keyword (**kwargs) parameters are not expanded into the mapping; the caller's kwargs mapping is merged as given. Unset parameters without a default cannot appear, because there is no value to report.

docs.title: Return annotations
docs.text:
list[str] None

Annotations are returned unevaluated. A string annotation (from __future__ import annotations) comes back as a string; resolve it with typing.get_type_hints if needed.

docs.title: Walking a class hierarchy
docs.text:
get_subclasses returns every descendant, not only direct children. Each class appears once, even when it is reachable through several branches, and the direct children keep their declaration order.

all: ['Left', 'Right', 'Leaf'] direct: ['Left', 'Right']

Subclasses are strong references

type.__subclasses__() keeps every subclass alive. Building classes dynamically in a long-running process keeps them registered for the lifetime of their base class.

docs.title: Serialization
docs.text: based_datatypes.serialize turns Python objects into two families of output — files and JSON-supported values — without the caller wiring up a library per format. You describe what you have and what you want; the package picks a serializer that understands both, tells you whether the format is lossless, and can estimate how large the result would be before you produce it.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• Serialize a dict, model, dataframe, array, image, XML tree or SQL statement without importing a different library for each format.
  • Convert values JSON cannot hold — datetime, complex, Decimal, UUID, bytes, enums — into something a JSON document can carry, and back again.
  • Read content back while declaring the type you expect, so a mismatched source fails loudly.
  • Ask for a lossless format when round-tripping matters, and accept a lossy one when it does not.
  • Budget an export before producing it.
  • Lay a serialized dictionary of files and primitives out as a directory tree.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
dict True { "hello": "world", "items": [ 1, 2 ] }

The serializer comes from the pair: the object's type and the requested target. A dict going to application/json picks the JSON serializer; a pandas.DataFrame to text/csv picks the dataframe serializer; a datetime picks the ISO 8601 serializer, because no file is involved.

docs.title: What can be serialized
docs.text:
Object Targets dict of JSON-shaped data JSON, YAML, itself pydantic.BaseModel JSON, YAML, dict of its dump pandas.DataFrame, polars.DataFrame CSV, parquet, Excel numpy.ndarray .npy, .npz, CSV PIL.Image.Image PNG, TIFF, BMP, JPEG, GIF, WebP xml.etree.ElementTree XML text, XML file bs4.BeautifulSoup HTML text, HTML file sqlalchemy statements SQL text, SQL file datetime, date, time ISO 8601 text timedelta a number of seconds complex a two-element [real, imaginary] list Decimal, uuid.UUID, pathlib.Path text bytes base64 text enum.Enum its value anything picklable pickle file

Optional formats need the common-serializers extra:

uv add "based-datatypes[common-serializers] @ git+https://github.com/cloudlane-one/based-datatypes.git"

It installs the serializer implementations (numpy, pandas+pyarrow+openpyxl, polars and its Excel backends, pillow, beautifulsoup4, sqlalchemy). Formats whose library is missing simply have no serializer, so selection reports no candidate instead of failing inside the serializer.

docs.title: Values JSON cannot hold
docs.text:
Scalars serialize to the primitive that carries them, so they can be embedded in a JSON document and read back with the annotation you expect:

datetime.datetime(2024, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5) -> '2024-01-02T03:04:05' datetime.date(2024, 1, 2) -> '2024-01-02' (3+4j) -> [3.0, 4.0] Decimal('1.10') -> '1.10' 2024-01-02 03:04:05 (3+4j) 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000001 aGVsbG8=

These serializers produce values, not files: a scalar has nothing to put in a file of its own. Embed it in a dictionary or list when you want it on disk.

docs.title: Reading back with an expected type
docs.text:
deserialize(source, annotation) validates what it parsed against the annotation. A source that does not fit raises TypeError; a pair of source and annotation that no serializer handles raises ValueError:

created: '2024-01-01T00:00:00' name: a

name='a' created=datetime.datetime(2024, 1, 1, 0, 0) refused: No suitable serializer found for LocalFile[typing.Literal['application/yaml'], , based_datatypes.files.Read | based_datatypes.files.Write] as list[int] under scope Open().

Model fields are converted with pydantic's JSON mode first, so datetime, UUID and Decimal values serialize instead of failing halfway through the write.

docs.title: Choosing a format
docs.text:
get_serializers(typ, targets, scope, lossless) returns the (index, target, driver) triples that can handle an object, ordered by the position of the matching target — the caller's first target wins. It is what serialize and deserialize use internally, and it is the way to ask which serializer would be picked. Passing value= matches the instance against each driver's declared object type as well, which is how a list of SQL statements is told apart from [1, 2]:

DateTimeSerializer, DateSerializer, PickleSerializer [] JSONSerializer handles dicts

docs.title: Lossless versus lossy formats
docs.text:
Some formats reproduce the object exactly, others keep only a reduced representation. A serializer declares which of its MIME types round-trip, because one serializer can cover both: parquet keeps a dataframe's dtypes and values, CSV does not; PNG is lossless, JPEG is not.

Pass lossless=True (the default) to require an exact round trip, lossless=False to accept a reduced one:

PdSerializer PdSerializer

Reading is not restricted this way: losslessness describes what an export can drop, so deserialize reads lossy formats as readily as lossless ones.

A target that is not a file has no MIME type to declare, so a serializer states that case separately with __lossless_values__; SQL and HTML declare False, because their text target is the same lossy re-rendering as their file. Without a requested target the filter is not applied at all — serialize(obj) takes the first format the serializer declares.

docs.title: Containers
docs.text:
A container — a mapping, a sequence, a set or a dataclass instance — reduces to a dictionary or a list, with every item serialized on its own. That is what turns values JSON cannot hold into a JSON-shaped payload: a datetime becomes its ISO 8601 text, a dataclass becomes a mapping of its fields, and an item that serializes to a file (a dataframe, an image) is nested as that file. The driver declares the dictionary and list value targets only, so a container that holds files is still a valid payload for a directory tree, while writing JSON or YAML files stays with JSONSerializer.

{'created': '2024-01-01T12:00:00'}

A serializer that cannot fulfil the requested target raises UnsupportedTargetError. serialize then tries the next matching serializer and raises only when none is left, so several drivers can declare the same format with different capabilities; a custom serializer implements that contract when it supports only some of the formats it declares.

docs.title: Declaring a scope
docs.text:
The third type argument of Serializer[V, T, S] declares the scope a serializer serves. A declaration serves a request when the request is an instance of the declared scope, and every scope derives from Open: an Open declaration therefore serves every request, while a declaration for a narrower scope cannot serve an unrestricted (Open) one. A serializer that leaves S out declares Open, which is why the built-in drivers are usable everywhere.

True

The declaration is a class, not a value: a scope carries data (a process id, a subnet), and only the caller knows it, so the value is supplied at call time while the class is what selection compares. The scope the caller passes is what a serializer and the ambient current_ser_ctx see — never the declaration.

docs.title: Estimating the export size
docs.text:
estimate_serialized_size(obj, target_type) reports how many bytes the serialization would produce, without writing anything. Speed wins over accuracy: an estimate only performs a full serialization when that serialization is the cheap route — a single C-level pass — and otherwise samples or bounds the payload.

Format Basis JSON exact, measured with the C encoder YAML the compact JSON payload, a rough upper bound (the YAML dumper is pure Python and ~150x slower) pydantic dumps the JSON-mode dump, measured like JSON XML exact, measured with the C serializer HTML a tag walk, about 10 % above the real size (rendering the soup is ~10x slower) SQL a strided sample of statements, formatted and extrapolated pickle exact, measured with the C pickler pandas/polars parquet in-memory / estimated size pandas, polars CSV sampled every n-th row and extrapolated .npy, .npz array payload plus the npy header images uncompressed pixel payload

estimated 39 written 39

docs.title: Writing a serialized dictionary as a directory tree
docs.text:
write_structure lays a dictionary of primitives and files out on disk:

  • primitives are collected in __index__.yaml inside the directory,
  • files are written next to it, named after their key,
  • nested dictionaries and lists become sub-directories named after their key,
  • the __index__.yaml of a list directory holds a YAML list, with None at the positions taken by files and sub-directories, whose files are named after their position.

['index.yaml', 'image.png', 'meta', 'size'] name: thumbnail

author: me

thumbnail [2, 2] {'author': 'me', 'tags': ['a', 'b']} image.png

Files read back as LocalFile handles, so they can be passed straight to deserialize. Rewriting a tree from its own structure (write_structure(read_structure(path), path)) is safe: each file's content is read before the entry it replaces is removed.

A key must be one path component and must not be __index__: the key decides a file name, so a key such as ../outside or an absolute path would write outside the tree, and __index__ would take the name of the index. Both raise ValueError before anything is created. Replacing a key with a value of another shape (a file over a sub-directory, a primitive over a file) removes the old artifact instead of leaving it to shadow the new value; keys the new structure does not mention are left in place.

docs.title: Writing a serializer for your own type
docs.text:
Subclass Serializer[YourType, TargetHint], implement serialize and deserialize, and register an instance. The class's type arguments are what selection reads, and each member of the target union becomes a declared format:

1.5,2.5 1.5,2.5 Point(1.5, 2.5)

CommonSerializer supplies the target handling: _resolve_target turns a target type or a file_factory into the file to write to, and returns None when the target is a plain value; __lossless_mimes__ declares which of the declared MIME types round-trip exactly, and __lossless_values__ whether the plain-value target does.

docs.title: The Serializable protocol
docs.text:
When the object itself knows how to serialize, implement the protocol instead of a serializer: __serialization_targets__, __deserialize__, __serialize__ and __estimate_serialized_size__. serialize, deserialize and estimate_serialized_size then dispatch to the object:

hello hello 5

docs.title: Traps worth knowing
docs.text:
• A target names its format. A bare File hint matches nothing: ask for File[Literal["application/json"], TextIO], or pass a file_factory and let the serializer pick its default format. The factory decides where the bytes go, the target type decides what they are.
  • A failed encode does not truncate an existing file. Text payloads are built before the target is opened, so a value the serializer rejects leaves the previous content intact.
  • Object arrays are refused for .npy/.npz. Writing them would require pickle and loading them would require allow_pickle=True; convert the array to a concrete dtype first.
  • Losslessness is per format, not per serializer. Asking for lossless=True with a CSV target has no candidate even though the same serializer writes lossless parquet.
  • A plain-value target can be lossy too. SQL and HTML re-render the object, so serialize(soup, str) needs lossless=False exactly like the .html file does.
  • A missing pair raises ValueError. serialize and deserialize name the object type, the target and the active scope in the message.

The public functions (serialize, deserialize, get_serializers, estimate_serialized_size, register_serializer, read_structure, write_structure), the Serializer and Serializable protocols, the scope classes and the shipped drivers are documented in the API reference and its submodules (base, common, local_fs).

docs.title: Shared types, markers and protocols
docs.text:
based_datatypes.types holds the small vocabulary the rest of the package (and its consumers) share: nominal string types, an unresolved-state enum, structural protocols, a named alias for ordered scalars, and a couple of typing helpers.

Nothing in this module performs I/O. Most names exist to make a type annotation precise at a call site without defining a class at that call site.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text: Reach for this module when a value needs a name (UUID4), when a function accepts "anything mapping-like" (SupportsItems), or when type reflection needs one of the helper protocols (DataclassInstance, StatePicklable, RuntimeValidated).

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text: UUID4 2f0c8d0e-8a5b-4f0e-9a1c-1d2e3f4a5b6c 'resolved' Attr(name='value')

docs.title: What the module holds
docs.text:
The names fall into four groups; their signatures and docstrings are in the API reference.

  • Nominal strings: UUID4.
  • State markers: Not (a StrEnum of defined, resolved, handled and changed), Undefined and ContraType.
  • Structural protocols: DataclassInstance, StatePicklable, ArgsPicklable, ArgsPicklableEx, RuntimeValidated, GenericAlias, LiteralGenericAlias, SupportsItems and SupportsKeysAndGetItem.
  • Shared aliases and vocabulary: Ordinal, Attr, operator_methods, and the type-expression unions TypeRoot, TypeNode, TypeMember, TypeDef, TypeScalar and TypeExpr that the typing helpers accept (plus AnnotationScanType and LiteralArg).

docs.title: Protocols are structural
docs.text:
The protocols are runtime_checkable, so they can be used with isinstance as runtime duck-typing checks.

True True True False

Protocol checks are shallow

isinstance on a runtime_checkable protocol only checks that the attributes exist, not their signatures. Use them for dispatch and diagnostics, not for validation.

docs.title: Nominal strings do not validate
docs.text:
UUID4 is a typing marker: constructing one accepts any string. Validate at the boundary where untrusted input enters (a pydantic model, for example), not by relying on the type.

not-a-uuid

docs.title: Ordered scalars
docs.text:
Ordinal names the set of types with a total order. It is a plain named alias, so it can be used directly in annotations and introspected with typing.get_args.

aliases: ['Decimal', 'bool', 'date', 'datetime', 'float', 'int', 'str', 'time', 'timedelta']

docs.title: Marker types
docs.text:
Undefined is a frozen dataclass, so all instances compare equal and hash alike. Use it as a default sentinel where None is a meaningful value.

ContraType carries a type object for contravariant APIs; the wrapped type is optional.

True

@final is static only

Undefined and ContraType are marked @final; Python does not prevent subclassing at runtime, the type checker does.

docs.title: Reflecting type hints at runtime
docs.text: based_datatypes.typing reads, normalises and compares type hints while the program runs. It is the layer that lets a framework answer questions such as "which concrete classes can this annotation produce?", "is this annotation a subtype of that one?", and "what are the type arguments of this generic class?".

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text: Use it when building serialisers, dependency injection, validation layers or generic base classes that need to know what an annotation means — not merely whether isinstance passes.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text: list[int] (,) True False

docs.title: API overview
docs.text: TypeRef is the entry point: it wraps a hint and exposes its origin, arguments, parameters, union members, resolved definition, type-variable map and validation, all cached. Runtyped adds the runtime record of type arguments to a class. Around them sit the predicates and helpers is_subtype, has_type, is_type_hint, get_lowest_common_base, get_inheritance_distance, is_frozen_dataclass, is_immutable, get_nondefault_methods and get_own_attrs, plus NoneType, OrderedSet and RepType. Signatures and docstrings are in the API reference; the sections below show how the pieces fit together.

docs.title: From a hint to concrete classes
docs.text:
TypeRef(...).typeset flattens unions, resolves named aliases and reduces parameterised generics to their origin. Literals, type variables and forward references carry no concrete class and contribute nothing.

{, } {} {} set() True True

docs.title: Subtyping and value checks
docs.text:
is_subtype understands generics, unions, Annotated, Literal and named aliases. has_type answers the value-level question.

True False True True True False

docs.title: Working with TypeRef
docs.text:
TypeRef is the workhorse: it resolves string and forward-reference hints, substitutes type variables, and exposes the pieces a framework needs. All properties are cached per reference.

Names True () (, ) scalar args: (, )

Use subs to replace open type variables and overrides when a replacement must take precedence over existing substitutions and defaults. pure_type_def removes Annotated metadata, while resolved_type_def retains it and recursively resolves type arguments:

list[~T] list[int] ('items',)

validate combines the runtime check with pydantic validation when the annotation carries it, and returns a boolean instead of raising:

True False False

Metadata only validates when pydantic can read it

Extra validation runs when the annotation is a pydantic FieldInfo or implements the RuntimeValidated protocol. Arbitrary Annotated metadata is ignored, exactly as isinstance would ignore it.

docs.title: Generic classes that know their arguments
docs.text:
Runtyped gives a class a runtime record of how it was parameterised. Sub[int] is a real, cached subclass that stores __origin__ and __args__, so the type arguments can be recovered later without rebuilding the generic machinery.

UserRepository (,) True resolved: ['int']

TypeRef reports the parameters a declaration is generic over, and resolves the parameters of a specialisation to the arguments it was applied with. Unapplied parameters resolve to their defaults, bounds, or Any:

K, V (, ) ['int', 'str']

Validation and subtyping compare these recorded arguments structurally. Thus a Box[int] instance does not validate as Box[str], even though a plain isinstance check cannot see the difference. Trailing arguments omitted from a supertype do not constrain the comparison.

docs.title: Replacing type variables
docs.text:
Pass a mapping of type variables to hints as subs. The same substitution is applied through nested arguments and generic bases. overrides is available for the less common case where a replacement must supersede substitutions and parameter defaults.

@contextmanager
def set_ctx_var[T](var: ContextVar[T], value: T) -> Generator[T]:
    """Set a context variable within a context manager, restoring the previous value on exit.

    Args:
        var: The context variable to set.
        value: The value to set the context variable to.

    Returns:
        A context manager that yields the set value.
    """
    token = var.set(value)
    try:
        yield value
    finally:
        var.reset(token)

def container_to_dict(
    container: Sequence | Set | Mapping | DataclassInstance | BaseModel,
    recursive: bool = True,
    _registry: dict[int, dict[Any, Any]] | None = None,
) -> dict[Any, Any] | None:
    """Turn an arbitrary container object into a dict.

    Args:
        container: The container to convert.
        recursive: Whether to recursively convert nested containers.
        _registry: Internal registry to track visited objects for cycle detection.

    Returns:
        A dict representation of the container, or None if not convertible.
    """
    _registry = _registry or {}

    obj_id = id(container)
    if obj_id in _registry:
        return _registry[obj_id]

    match container:
        case DataclassInstance():
            res = {
                Attr(f_name): getattr(container, f_name)
                for f_name in container.__dataclass_fields__.keys()
            }
        case _ if isinstance(container, BaseModel):
            res = {Attr(k): v for k, v in container.model_dump().items()}
        case Mapping():
            res = dict(container)
        case str() | bytes() | bytearray():
            # Scalars are iterable, but not containers to be indexed.
            return None
        case Iterable():
            res = {i: v for i, v in enumerate(container)}
        case _:
            return None

    _registry[obj_id] = res

    if recursive:
        for k, v in list(res.items()):
            m = container_to_dict(v, True, _registry)
            res[k] = m if m is not None else v

    return res

def copy_and_override[**Params, DC: DataclassInstance](
    _init: Callable[Params, DC] | MaskedInit[Params, DC] | type[DC],
    _obj: DataclassInstance | tuple[DataclassInstance, ...],
    *args: Params.args,
    **kwargs: Params.kwargs,
) -> DC:
    """Re-construct a dataclass instance with all its init params + override.

    Args:
        _init: The dataclass constructor or a `MaskedInit` wrapping it.
        _obj: The dataclass instance(s) to copy values from.
        *args: Positional arguments to override.
        **kwargs: Keyword arguments to override.

    Returns:
        A new dataclass instance with the specified overrides.

    Note:
        Required attributes of the target dataclass type must always be provided as args / kwargs.

    Warning:
        Does not work for kw_only dataclasses and InitVars (yet).
    """
    if isinstance(_init, MaskedInit):
        _init = _init.constructor
    if not isinstance(_init, type):
        orig_init = get_origin(_init)
        assert orig_init is not None
        _init = orig_init

    constr_func = cast(Callable[..., DC], _init)
    target_fields = list(fields(cast(type, _init)))

    objs = _obj if isinstance(_obj, tuple) else (_obj,)

    obj_fields: dict[Field, Any] = {}
    for obj in objs:
        src_fields = set(f.name for f in obj.__dataclass_fields__.values())
        all_obj_fields = {f: getattr(obj, f.name) for f in target_fields if f.name in src_fields}
        obj_fields = {
            f: (
                v
                if v is not MISSING
                else obj_fields.get(
                    f,
                    (
                        f.default
                        if f.default is not MISSING
                        else (f.default_factory() if f.default_factory is not MISSING else MISSING)
                    ),
                )
            )
            for f, v in all_obj_fields.items()
        }

    assert not any(v is MISSING for v in obj_fields.values())

    obj_kwargs = list({f.name: v for f, v in obj_fields.items() if f.init}.items())
    new_kwargs = {
        **dict(obj_kwargs[len(args) :] if len(args) < len(obj_kwargs) else {}),
        **kwargs,
    }

    new_obj = constr_func(*args, **new_kwargs)  # pyright: ignore[reportCallIssue]

    for f, v in obj_fields.items():
        if not f.init:
            setattr(new_obj, f.name, v)

    return new_obj

def flatten_dict(
    d: Mapping[Any, Any],
    path: tuple = (),
    _registry: dict[int, dict[tuple, Any]] | None = None,
) -> dict[tuple, Any]:
    """Turn a nested mapping into a flat dict (ignoring recursive references).

    Args:
        d: The mapping to flatten.
        path: The current path of keys (used for recursion).
        _registry: Internal registry to track visited objects for cycle detection.

    Returns:
        A flat dict mapping tuple paths to values.
    """
    items: dict[tuple, Any] = {}

    _registry = _registry or {}

    obj_id = id(d)
    if obj_id in _registry:
        return _registry[obj_id]

    _registry[obj_id] = items

    for k, v in d.items():
        new_path = path + (k,)
        if isinstance(v, Mapping):
            items.update(flatten_dict(v, new_path, _registry))
        else:
            items[new_path] = v

    return items

def cached_method[S, R, **P](
    func: Callable[Concatenate[S, P], R],
) -> Callable[Concatenate[S, P], R]:
    """Decorator to cache method results on the instance level."""

    @functools.wraps(func)
    def wrapper(self: S, *args: P.args, **kwargs: P.kwargs) -> R:
        # ``vars`` is the receiver's own namespace, so a subclass never reuses a
        # cache an ancestor stored: inherited attributes would hide it from
        # ``hasattr`` and let classmethod caches leak down the MRO.
        cache_name = f"__{func.__name__}_cache"
        namespace = vars(self)
        if cache_name not in namespace:
            setattr(self, cache_name, {})

        # The function is part of the key: a decorated override and the decorated
        # base method it calls through ``super()`` share one cache attribute per
        # name, and without the function the override's result would be returned
        # for the base implementation too.
        cache: dict[tuple[Any, ...], R] = namespace[cache_name]
        key = (func, args, frozenset(kwargs.items()))

        if key not in cache:
            cache[key] = func(self, *args, **kwargs)

        return cache[key]

    return wrapper

def get_module_distribution(module: ModuleType) -> meta.Distribution | None:
    """Get the distribution package of given module, if any.

    Args:
        module: Module to inspect.

    Returns:
        Distribution package of the module, or ``None`` if not part of a distribution.
    """
    mod_file = get_module_file(module)
    if mod_file is None:
        return None

    dists = {
        Path(str(dist.locate_file(f"{name}"))): dist for name, dist in get_distributions().items()
    }

    # An editable install resolves to the repository root, which contains the
    # whole virtual environment; the most specific (deepest) match wins so a
    # module in ``site-packages`` is attributed to its own distribution.
    mod_dists: list[tuple[int, meta.Distribution]] = []
    for dist_path, dist in dists.items():
        if mod_file.is_relative_to(dist_path):
            mod_dists.append((len(dist_path.parts), dist))
        elif dist.origin is not None and "url" in dist.origin.__dict__:  # type: ignore
            url = str(dist.origin.url)
            if url.startswith("file://"):
                path = _file_url_to_path(url)
                if mod_file.is_relative_to(path):
                    mod_dists.append((len(path.parts), dist))

    if len(mod_dists) == 0:
        return None

    return max(mod_dists, key=lambda item: item[0])[1]

    Args:
        dist: Distribution to inspect.

    if dist.metadata is None:

    proj_urls = dist.metadata.get_all("Project-URL")
    if proj_urls is None:

    proj_urls_split = [str(url).split(", ") for url in proj_urls]

    if len(urls) == 0:

    return urls

        docs_url: Documentation URL to fetch inventory from.

    inv_url = f"{docs_url.rstrip('/')}/objects.inv"

    inv_dict = inv.InventoryFile.load(

def get_io(self, mode: Literal["rw", "r", "w"] = "rw") -> I:
    """Return a stream over the file's content.

    Writes are stored back into :attr:`content` when the stream is closed.
    ``"w"`` and ``"rw"`` start from empty content, like a local file, while
    ``"r"`` starts from the current content and rejects writes.

    initial = self.content if mode == "r" else None

            I,
            _TextMemoryStream(
                self,
                cast(str, initial) if initial is not None else "",
                writable=writable,

        )

    return cast(
        I,
        _BinaryMemoryStream(
            self,
            cast(bytes, initial) if initial is not None else b"",
            writable=writable,
        ),
    )

def ensure_dir_exists(path: Path | str) -> Path:
    """Make sure the given path exists and is a directory.

    Create dir if necessary. Then return the path unchanged.

    Args:
        path: Path to ensure exists.

    Returns:
        The given path.
    """
    path = Path(path).absolute()
    p = Path(path.parts[0])
    for d in path.parts[1:]:
        p = p / d
        if not p.is_dir():
            if not p.exists():
                p.mkdir()
            else:
                raise NotADirectoryError()

    return path

@_hashing_context
def gen_int_hash(_ctx: set[int], obj: Any) -> int:  # noqa: C901
    """Generate stable hash for obj (must be known, hashable or composed of such).

    Args:
        obj: Object to hash.

    Returns:
        Hash of the object as integer.
    """
    match obj:
        case None:
            return 0
        case ModuleType():
            return gen_int_hash(obj.__name__)
        case type() | TypeAliasType():
            return gen_int_hash((obj.__module__, obj.__name__))
        case FunctionType() if hasattr(obj, "__name__"):
            return gen_int_hash(str(PyObjectRef.reference(obj).url))
        case FunctionType():
            # This may be unstable as closures are not considered.
            return gen_int_hash(list(obj.__code__.co_lines()))
        case GenericAlias() | UnionType():
            base = get_origin(obj)
            args = get_args(obj)
            return gen_int_hash(
                (
                    (
                        "types.UnionType"
                        if base is UnionType
                        else str(PyObjectRef.reference(base).url)
                    ),
                    *(gen_int_hash(arg) for arg in args),
                )
            )
        case Number() | str() | bytes() | date() | time() | datetime() | timedelta():
            return _stable_hash(obj)
        case tuple():
            return _hash_sequence(obj, _ctx)
        case _ if id(obj) in _ctx:
            return 0
        case _ if isinstance(obj, pd.DataFrame | pd.Series | pd.Index):
            # pandas types ``hash_pandas_object`` loosely, hence the ignore.
            return sum(hash_pandas_object(obj))  # pyright: ignore[reportCallIssue]
        case list():
            _ctx.add(id(obj))
            return _hash_sequence(obj, _ctx)
        case dict():
            _ctx.add(id(obj))
            return sum(_hash_sequence(item, _ctx) for item in obj.items())
        case set():
            _ctx.add(id(obj))
            return sum(gen_int_hash(item) for item in obj)
        case Hashable():
            _ctx.add(id(obj))
            return hash(obj)
        case DataclassInstance():
            _ctx.add(id(obj))
            return gen_int_hash({f.name: getattr(obj, f.name) for f in fields(obj)})
        # ``object`` has provided ``__getstate__`` since Python 3.11, so the
        # protocol alone matches every instance; require a custom state hook.
        case StatePicklable() if type(obj).__getstate__ is not object.__getstate__:
            state = obj.__getstate__()
            state = state if isinstance(state, tuple) else (state,)
            state_dicts = [s for s in state if isinstance(s, dict)]

            if len(state_dicts) == 0:
                raise ValueError()

            return sum(sum(_hash_sequence((k, v), _ctx) for k, v in s.items()) for s in state_dicts)
        case ArgsPicklable():
            args = obj.__getnewargs__()
            return sum(gen_int_hash(item) for item in args)
        case ArgsPicklableEx():
            args, kwargs = obj.__getnewargs_ex__()
            return sum(gen_int_hash(item) for item in args) + sum(
                gen_int_hash(item) for item in kwargs.items()
            )
        case _:
            if pl is not None:
                match obj:
                    case pl.DataFrame():
                        return sum(obj.hash_rows()) if not obj.is_empty() else 0
                    case pl.Series():
                        return sum(obj.hash())
                    case _:
                        pass

            raise ValueError()

@staticmethod
def from_url(url_text: str, obj_type: type[T]) -> "PyObjectRef[T]":
    """Create a reference from given URL.

    Args:
        url_text: URL text to parse.
        obj_type: Type of the referenced object.

    Returns:
        Reference to the object.
    """
    url = URL(url_text)

    repo_url = None
    if url.scheme.startswith("py+"):
        # Version and Python constraints are carried as query parameters,
        # so they must not leak into the repository URL.
        repo_url = str(
            URL.build(
                scheme=url.scheme[3:],
                host=url.host or "",
                port=url.port,
                path=url.path,
            )
        )

    if ":" not in url.fragment:
        raise ValueError(
            f"URL fragment must be of the form '<module>:<qualname>', got '{url.fragment}'."
        )

    module, object = url.fragment.split(":", 1)  # Split module and object

    return PyObjectRef(
        object_type=obj_type,
        repo_url=repo_url,
        version=url.query.get("version"),
        py_version=url.query.get("python"),
        module_name=module,
        qualname=object,
    )

@staticmethod
def reference(  # noqa: C901
    obj: T2,
    version: str | None = None,
    version_strategy: VersionStrategy = "major",
) -> "PyObjectRef[T2]":
    """Create a reference to given object.

    Args:
        obj: Object to create reference for.
        version: Exact or range version specifier for the object's package/repo.
        version_strategy: Strategy to use for version range specification.

    Returns:
        Reference to the given object.
    """
    qualname = getattr(obj, "__qualname__", None)
    if qualname is None:
        raise ValueError("Object must have fully qualified name (`__qualname__`)")

    module = inspect.getmodule(obj)
    if module is None:
        raise ValueError("Object must be associated with a module.")

    dist = get_module_distribution(module)
    package = dist.name if dist is not None else None

    git_repo = None
    repo = None

    if dist is not None and dist.origin is not None:
        # Fetch the origin URL of the distribution, if any.
        repo = dict(dist.origin.__dict__).get("url")

    if dist is None or str(repo).startswith("file://"):
        # Not part of distribution or local file origin URL
        # -> assume first-party code commited to Git repo.
        git_repo = get_module_repo(module)
        if git_repo is not None:
            repo = git_repo.remote().url

    if repo is None:
        if dist is not None:
            # Code is part of distribution, but no explicit origin URL
            # -> assume PyPI indexed package
            repo = f"https://pypi.org/simple/{package}"
        elif module.__name__ != "builtins":
            # No distribution, no Git repo and not built-in module
            raise ValueError("Non-builtin object must be associated with a repository.")

    version_exact = None
    semver_exact = None

    if version is None:
        if dist is not None:
            version_exact = dist.version
            try:
                semver_exact = Version(version_exact)
            except InvalidVersion:
                pass
        elif git_repo is not None:
            current_tags = [tag for tag in git_repo.tags if tag.commit == git_repo.head.commit]
            if len(current_tags) > 0:
                for tag in current_tags:
                    version_exact = tag.name
                    try:
                        semver_exact = Version(version_exact)
                        break
                    except InvalidVersion:
                        continue
            elif not git_repo.head.is_detached:
                version_exact = git_repo.active_branch.name
                try:
                    semver_exact = Version(version_exact)
                except InvalidVersion:
                    pass

    if semver_exact is not None:
        version = version_to_range(semver_exact, version_strategy)
    elif version_strategy == "exact" and version_exact is not None:
        version = f"=={version_exact}"

    return PyObjectRef(
        object_type=type(obj),
        qualname=qualname,
        module_name=module.__name__,
        repo_url=repo,
        version=version,
        py_version=version_to_range(Version(f"{platform.python_version()}"), "minor"),
        _module=module,
        _dist=dist,
        _object=obj,
    )

def get_all_module_dependencies(
    module: ModuleType,
    _ext_deps: set[str] | None = None,
    _int_deps: set[ModuleType] | None = None,
) -> tuple[set[str], set[ModuleType]]:
    """Return all (indirect) dependency modules of given module.

    Args:
        module: Module to inspect.

    Returns:
        Tuple of external and internal dependencies.
    """
    if _ext_deps is None:
        _ext_deps = set()
    if _int_deps is None:
        # Seed with the module itself so a dependency cycle does not report
        # the entry point as one of its own dependencies.
        _int_deps = {module}

    deps = [dep for _, m in inspect.getmembers(module) if (dep := inspect.getmodule(m)) is not None]
    ext_deps_map = {
        dep: dist.metadata["Name"]
        for dep in deps
        if (dist := get_module_distribution(dep)) is not None and dist.metadata is not None
    }
    new_ext_deps = set(ext_deps_map.values()) - _ext_deps

    these_int_deps = set(deps) - set(ext_deps_map.keys())
    new_int_deps = these_int_deps - _int_deps

    if len(new_ext_deps) > 0 or len(new_int_deps) > 0:
        _ext_deps |= new_ext_deps
        _int_deps |= new_int_deps

        for dependency in new_int_deps:
            sub_ext_deps, sub_int_deps = get_all_module_dependencies(
                dependency, _ext_deps, _int_deps
            )
            _ext_deps |= sub_ext_deps
            _int_deps |= sub_int_deps

        return _ext_deps, _int_deps - {module}

    return _ext_deps, _int_deps - {module}

def get_outdated_deps(
    dist: meta.Distribution | ModuleType,
    allowed_diff: Specifier = Specifier("<=1.1.1"),
) -> dict[str, tuple[Version, Version]]:
    """Get a list of outdated dependencies of a distribution.

    Args:
        dist:
            Distribution to inspect.
            Can also be supplied as a module within the distribution in question.
        allowed_diff: Allowed difference between current and latest version.

    Returns:
        Dictionary of outdated package names with current and latest version.
    """
    if isinstance(dist, ModuleType):
        mod_dist = get_module_distribution(dist)
        if mod_dist is None:
            raise ValueError("Supplied module is not part of a distribution.")
        dist = mod_dist

    deps = get_dist_requirements(dist)

    if deps is None:
        return {}

    outdated = {}
    for dep in deps:
        try:
            dep_dist = meta.distribution(dep.name)
        except meta.PackageNotFoundError:
            dep_dist = dep.name

        versions = get_versions_on_pypi(dep_dist)
        versions = {
            v
            for v in versions
            if not v.is_prerelease and not v.is_postrelease and not v.is_devrelease
        }

        matching_req = set(dep.specifier.filter(versions))
        newest_matching = max(matching_req)

        newer = versions - matching_req
        if len(newer) == 0:
            continue

        newest = max(newer)
        diff = version_diff(newest, newest_matching)
        if diff is not None and diff not in allowed_diff:
            outdated[dep.name] = (newest_matching, newest)

    return outdated

def get_versions_on_pypi(package: meta.Distribution | str) -> set[Version]:
    """Get all available versions of given distribution.

    Args:
        package: Distribution or package name to inspect.

    Returns:
        Set of available versions.

    if isinstance(package, meta.Distribution):
        if package.origin is not None:
            return set()
        package = package.name

    url = f"https://pypi.org/pypi/{package}/json"

    response = requests.get(url)
    if response.status_code == 404:
        return set()

    data = response.json()

    versions = set()
    for v in data["releases"].keys():
        try:
            versions.add(Version(v))
        except InvalidVersion:
            pass

    return versions

def semver_range_to_spec(semver_range: str) -> SpecifierSet:
    """Convert semver range to Python version specifier.

    Args:
        semver_range: Semver range string.

    Returns:
        Corresponding Python version specifier set.
    """
    match = re.match(r"^(?P<op>\^|~|>=|<=|==|=|>|<)?(?P<version>.+)$", semver_range.strip())
    if match is None:
        raise ValueError(f"Invalid semver range: '{semver_range}'.")

    op = match.group("op")
    version = Version(match.group("version").strip())

    if op == "^":
        return SpecifierSet(f">={version.public},<{version.major + 1}")

    if op == "~":
        return SpecifierSet(f">={version.public},<{version.major}.{version.minor + 1}")

    if op in (">=", "<=", ">", "<"):
        return SpecifierSet(f"{op}{version.public}")

    return SpecifierSet(f"=={version.public}")

def version_diff(v1: Version, v2: Version) -> Version | None:
    """Get the difference between two versions (v1 - v2).

    Args:
        v1: Newer version.
        v2: Older version.

    Returns:
        Difference between ``v1`` and ``v2`` as Version, or ``None`` if ``v1 < v2``
    """
    if v1 < v2:
        return None

    v1_arr = (v1.major, v1.minor, v1.micro)
    v2_arr = (v2.major, v2.minor, v2.micro)

    diff = tuple(a - b for a, b in zip(v1_arr, v2_arr))

    if diff[0] > 0:
        diff = (diff[0], v1_arr[1], v1_arr[2])
    elif diff[1] > 0:
        diff = (diff[0], diff[1], v1_arr[2])

    return Version(".".join(str(v) for v in diff))

def get_full_args_dict(
    func: Callable, args: Sequence, kwargs: dict[str, Any] | None = None
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Return dict of all args + kwargs.

    Args:
        func: Function to inspect.
        args: Positional arguments given to the function.
        kwargs: Keyword arguments given to the function.

    Returns:
        Dictionary of all args + kwargs.
    """
    argspec = inspect.getfullargspec(func)

    posonlyargs = list(getattr(argspec, "posonlyargs", ()))
    posarg_names = [*posonlyargs, *argspec.args]

    arg_defaults = argspec.defaults or []
    defaulted_names = posarg_names[len(posarg_names) - len(arg_defaults) :]
    defaults = dict(zip(defaulted_names, arg_defaults))
    defaults |= dict(argspec.kwonlydefaults or {})

    # Handle bound methods
    if len(posarg_names) > 0 and posarg_names[0] == "self" and hasattr(func, "__self__"):
        posarg_names = posarg_names[1:]

    posargs = dict(zip(posarg_names[: len(args)], args))

    return {**defaults, **posargs, **(kwargs or {})}

def get_subclasses[T](cls: type[T], max_level: int | None = None, _level: int = 1) -> list[type[T]]:
    """Return all subclasses of given class.

    Args:
        cls: The class to get subclasses for.
        max_level: Maximum inheritance level to traverse.
        _level: Current inheritance level (for internal use).

    Returns:
        List of subclasses.
    """
    if max_level is not None and _level > max_level:
        return []

    subclasses = list(dict.fromkeys(cls.__subclasses__()))

    for subclass in cls.__subclasses__():
        for sub_subclass in get_subclasses(subclass, max_level=max_level, _level=_level + 1):
            if sub_subclass not in subclasses:
                subclasses.append(sub_subclass)

@staticmethod
def match(
    targets: Iterable[SerializationTarget[Any, Any, Any]],
    types: Collection[TypeDef[Serialized]] | None = None,
    scope: TransportScope | None = None,
    lossless: bool = True,
) -> list[SerializationTarget[T, S, L]]:
    """Return the subset of targets that match any of the given types.

    Args:
        targets: The list of serialization targets to filter.
        types: The collection of types to match against.
        scope: The scope to match.
        lossless: Whether to only include lossless targets.

    Returns:
        The list of matching serialization targets.
    """
    return cast(
        list[SerializationTarget[T, S, L]],
        [
            t
            for t in targets
            if (
                any((TypeRef(tt).is_subtype_of(t.type)) for tt in types)
                if types is not None
                else True
            )
            and (_scope_serves(t.scope, scope) if scope is not None else True)
            and (not lossless or t.lossless)
        ],
    )

def lossless_target(cls, hint: TypeDef[Any]) -> bool:
    """Whether a target format round-trips the object exactly.

    A file target does exactly when all of its MIME types are declared
    lossless by the serializer; a target that is not a file follows

    mimes = target_mimes(hint)

def match(self, scopes: Collection[TransportScope | type[TransportScope]]) -> bool:
    """Check whether this declared scope can serve any of the requested scopes.

    The declaration is the receiver and the requests are the arguments: a
    declaration serves a request when the request is an instance of the
    declared scope, so a serializer declared for :class:`Open` serves every
    request, while one declared for a narrower scope cannot serve an
    unrestricted one. Scopes form a hierarchy rooted at :class:`Open`, and
    the comparison is the class relation, never an exact-class match.

    Args:
        scopes: The requested scopes, as classes or values.

    Returns:
        ``True`` if this declaration can serve at least one request.
    """
    return any(_scope_serves(self, scope) for scope in scopes)
